lesson.title: Learning in the Dark: What Tolman's Rats Revealed
lesson.summary: Latent learning is learning that happens without any obvious reward and stays hidden until there's a reason to show it, and Tolman and Honzik's classic maze experiment is the clearest demonstration of the effect.
lesson.body:
Cognitive maps suggest that animals build internal representations of their environment as they explore it, whether or not anything rewarding happens along the way. Latent learning is the direct behavioral proof of that idea: learning that occurs without reinforcement and doesn't show up in performance until there's a reason, usually a reward, to demonstrate it.

In Tolman and Honzik's classic 1930 study, three groups of rats ran the same maze once a day. One group found food at the goal box every single run, and their error rate dropped steadily over the following days, a straightforward result of ordinary reinforcement. A second group never found food at all, and these rats kept wandering the maze with a persistently high error rate, showing little apparent improvement. A third group ran unrewarded for about the first ten days, just like the second group, and then began receiving food at the goal starting on day eleven.

What happened to that third group is the heart of the finding. Within a day or two of the food first appearing, their error rate dropped sharply, falling to match or nearly match the rats that had been rewarded from the very first day. That kind of overnight improvement makes no sense if those rats had genuinely learned nothing during their first ten unrewarded runs. It makes complete sense if they had already been building an accurate cognitive map of the maze the whole time; they simply had no reason to rush efficiently toward the goal box until food gave them one.

This is the clearest illustration of the learning-versus-performance distinction that also came up with observational learning: what an organism has learned and what it currently shows in its behavior are not the same thing, and behavior only reveals learning once there's sufficient motivation to display it. The everyday version of this is familiar: someone who has casually wandered a new mall or campus with no particular goal often turns out, when they later actually need to find a specific store or room quickly, to know the layout far better than they realized, because they'd been building the map all along.
